title: 'Gateless Barrier, Case 27: Nansen''s "Not Mind, Not Buddha, Not Things"'
speaker: Kanshin Allison Tate
summary: In this dharma talk, Alison explores the concept of reality as constantly changing and impermanent, encouraging us to let go of attachments to fixed ideas about ourselves or the world around us. We often cling to concepts like a permanent "everyday mind" or a safe "Buddha," but true understanding reveals that these are just illusions. By embracing this ever-changing nature of reality, we can begin to see beyond our conceptual frameworks and rest in the present moment, unencumbered by attachments to identity or permanence.
topics: Sheng Yan's teaching on individualized meditation methods

sentences.text: Good morning everybody.
Am I audible all the way to the back of the room?
For those of you who don't know me, I'm Alison, Kanshin Allison Tate.
As of September, I've been the resident teacher at Seattle Soto Zen.
I think Tim mentioned yesterday that I echo Jeff Kelly, who'd been the guiding teacher there for ten years.
He had to step down for his health, so I stepped up.
I really want to thank Red Cedar Zen for inviting the Seattle Sangha to share this Rohatsu sesshin with you and for hosting us in your beautiful zendo.
I'm only a little bit envious.
I'd really like to thank Tim for inviting me to co-lead with him and to give this talk today.

So today I'm going to continue the exploration of the gateless barrier, the Mumunkan, and I'll be speaking on case 27, which would have made perfect sense if we hadn't recently gone off script and skipped over 24 and 26.
And by we, of course, I mean Tim.
But we go on. 27 it is.
So case 27: Nonsens, not mind, not Buddha, not things.
A monk asked Nonsen, "Is there any dharma that has not been preached to the people?"
Nonsen answered, "There is."
"What is the truth that has not been taught as a monk?"
Nonsen said, "It is not mind.
It is not Buddha.
It is not things."

And Mumun's comment on this case is, "At this question, Nonsen used up all his treasure and was left destitute," which kind of brings us back to yesterday's case of leaping from the top of the 100-foot pole, because that's what we do, right?
We collect this huge heap of merit by doing ridiculous things like sitting sesshin, and we collect all this knowledge.
And for what end?
So that we can give it away freely to whoever comes and asks for it.
So this is what Nonsen did when he answered this question.
The monk asked, "Can you give me whatever you haven't given me already?"
And it sounds like Nonsen had already given him the mind, Buddha, and things, which is a lot to give somebody.
But when the monk said, "Can you give me something else?" he gave him not mind, not Buddha, not things.
And that was all he had to give.
So this is his heroic leap, giving everything to the monk only because the monk asked.
I'll read the case one more time, probably a couple more times, but one more time right now.
A monk asked Nonsen, "Is there any Dharma that has not been preached to the people?"
Nonsen answered, "There is."
"What is the truth that has not been taught?" asked the monk.
Nonsen said, "It is not mind.
It is not Buddha.
It is not things."
So you probably recognize Nonsen from a much more popular case that he features in, which is when he spoke to Joshu.
And he said, Joshu asked, "What is the way?" and Nonsen replied, "Ordinary mind is the way," or "everyday mind is the way," because Norman's preferred translation.
And now he says, "Not mind, not Buddha, not things."

So I don't think it's a contradiction to "everyday mind is the way," because when we, I think, when I study cases like "everyday mind is the way" or "Mahasutra, this very mind is Buddha," I think I get it, but I'm pretty sure it's a wrong understanding.
Because when I believe that "everyday mind is the way," it's not really this very mind here and now.
Because for one thing, by the time I finish saying "this very mind here and now," it's already a different mind.

And it's also when I believe that "this very mind is the way" or "it was Buddha," it's, I don't think that when I'm yelling at my partner or stuck in traffic, I tend to think "mind is Buddha" when I'm having a really great meditation experience or come across a sudden waterfall and a hike in the mountains, which is not this very mind.
It's not "everyday mind," because "everyday mind" is really "everyday mind."
It'd be like if I took a jar down to the river and carried it around with me and said, "Look, I've got the Nooksack River in my bag."
That's not the river, that's just a jar of water, Alison.
So it's like that.
When we say "ordinary mind is the way," it's an ordinary mind that is always changing over, which is the way.
And because it's always changing, it's also not mind and not the way and not Buddha and not things.
And when I think of "not things," I remember years ago, this was before orca cards were invented.
And you used to go to the store and get a monthly bus pass each month.
And a friend of mine was leaving a Dharma study and she dropped her bus pass.
So I picked it up and ran after her.
I said, "Oh, you lost your bus pass, you won't get far without this."
And she took it back for me.
And she said, "Well, thank you very much."
But "this isn't a bus pass, it's a bookmark."
Because as happened this year, December kind of snuck up on me.
So I didn't realize that it was actually in the new month.
So the bus pass wouldn't take you anywhere anymore.
Because we'd just been studying Zen together in our book club.
It that really was a real moment for me.
Yeah, also, in the workplace, I tend to get along pretty well with my younger coworkers, probably because I'm kind of immature.
I remember this one workplace where one of these younger coworkers, a young woman in her early 20s, she got sent home for wearing leggings to work.
This was before everyone was wearing leggings everywhere.
And the boss said, "Well, you can't wear that in the workplace because leggings aren't pants."
And you know, she was really mad.
She didn't believe him.
There was like a real division in the workplace between the people, like over 30, people under 30, on why their leggings were pants.
And, you know, obviously, the under 30s one because now everyone's wearing leggings everywhere.
I think that's, I think it's a very good thing to remember that things are also not things.
I think this time of year really brings it out of them.
But I have some older relations who get really upset that certain films or books or ideas that they had in their youth aren't socially acceptable anymore, but they're actually racist.
And, you know, they're furious when that's pointed out because, you know, "this is my treasured memory."
This book comes along with all of these associations that are so pleasant.
So they need to defend that book and themselves.
And, you know, I kind of, I've had that feeling too.
And I think because of my practice, I don't have this same need to defend my ground because things are always arising here, passing away, and then arising somewhere else in a different form.
So it can be, it can be both.
It can be a treasured memory and a very offensive story.
I don't have to choose.
There's actually none of them.

The Diamond Sutra very famously says that "present mind cannot be grasped, past mind cannot be grasped, and future mind cannot be grasped" because it's this constantly flowing stream where thoughts aren't really thoughts, things aren't really things, and they're coming in and out of existence.
So I didn't have too much trouble with "not mind and not things."
But for some reason, the teaching of "not Buddha" is a little more difficult for me, I think.
You know, as you know from the past talks on the Mumunkan, a lot of monks asked their teachers, "What is Buddha?"
I don't remember too many besides this one that asked, "What is not Buddha?"
And as you know, so I think probably about a month ago, Tim would have presented Mumunkan case 21, which has said "Buddha is toilet paper."
So Buddha is so many things, but "what is not Buddha?"
And I think, I think I kind of want Buddha to be everything, to be permanent and safe and not changing around too much.
But that's not a very useful Buddha, right?
Because if people and things are constantly changing and Buddha stays the same, then Buddha isn't really relevant for long.
I think this longing for permanence and, you know, some sort of eternal existence, I don't think it's really what we want.
I think we're more afraid of the alternative.
It's American novelist Susan Ertz who said, "Millions long for immortality who don't know what to do with themselves on a rainy Sunday afternoon."
So what's the way now?
How do we understand "not mind and not Buddha and not things?"
Now I'm going to suggest that one way is by careful examination of mind, Buddha and things.
Probably the most famous phrase from the Shobogenzo, "to study the Buddha way is to study the self."
To study the self is to forget the self.
And to forget the self is to be awakened by myriad things.
In this case also awakened by myriad not things.
And I actually have a story that is about forgetting the self by studying the self.
This is teaching of Sheng Yan.
Master Sheng Yan was of Chinese heritage.
He studied in his youth with Chan masters.
And then a lot of things happened, including him being drafted in the army for several years.
And later he went on to study with other masters in Japan.
So he's a teacher in both sort of a Chinese Rinzai tradition and a Japanese Soto tradition, which gave him kind of a really unique perspective on teaching and on him being a teacher.
And one of the ways he instructed his students was that in sitting meditation he would assign the student a meditation method based on his perception of their affinities.
So they'd all be sitting together in a dharma hall like we are now.
And some students would be sitting with the koan, well actually wado, but basically the same thing as a koan.
And some would be counting breaths and some would be sitting shikantaza.
And strangely enough, a lot of his students weren't happy with the meditation method that they were assigned and thought that the master had given them the wrong one.
So there was a lot of grumbling about it.
And Master Sheng Yan's response was he said to completely devote yourself to whatever method you've been assigned.
And he said it's like following a path.
At the beginning the path is very narrow and it's hard to walk it.
But as we walk it, the path widens.
So it's much easier to diverse.
And then finally the path, we lose the path again, but not because we've gone off track but because the path has widened so much that our entire field is the path.
And in this way the path is no path.
Whenever he's said that several times and it's in a lot of his books and the collections of his teachings.
And whenever I read that, I think of a famous poem by Rumi, "A Great Wagon."
So this is just an excerpt.
*Out beyond ideas of wrongdoing and rightdoing, there is a field.
I'll meet you there.
When the soul lies down in that grass the world is too full to talk about.
Ideas, language, even the phrase each other don't make any sense.
The breeze at dawn has secrets to tell you.
Don't go back to sleep.
You must ask for what you really want.
Don't go back to sleep.
People are going back and forth across the door sill where the two worlds touch.
The door is round and open.
Don't go back to sleep.* So I think of the place where the path widens until there's no longer a path.
There's no longer a path.
To me that feels like the field beyond ideas of wrongdoing and rightdoing.
So all of us, wherever, whatever path we're following, it's my own path.
I'm completely devoted to it.
And it ends in this beautiful field with everyone else who follows their own path and great devotion and sincerity.
*Out beyond ideas of wrongdoing and rightdoing, there is a field.
I'll meet you there.
When the soul lies down in that grass the world is too full to talk about.
Ideas, language, even the phrase each other don't make any sense.
The breeze at dawn has secrets to tell you.
Don't go back to sleep.
You must ask for what you really want.
Don't go back to sleep.
People are going back and forth across the door sill where the two worlds touch.
The door is round and open.
Don't go back to sleep.* And I think this teaching, "what is the truth that is not being taught," it is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not things.
That it's also, it's not, it's not just negation.
I think Nansen is really talking about not mind, not Buddha, and not things.
Like the koan that starts the Mumunkan.
Joshu says, "No.
This is the dog have buddha nature."
Joshu says, "No."
And practicing with that koan is really living with "no."
So it's sitting down for a cup of tea and inviting "no" to sit down across from me.
And with this intimacy with "no," at a certain point the teacher asks some probing questions which don't make a lot of sense, like "what, so what colour is no?"
Or "how tall is no?"
And so there's this real intimacy with "no" where it isn't just negation, it's it's "no."
It's a "no" that has an existence that I live with very, very closely.
So practicing, it's kind of like going around all day saying "no, no, no," like a toddler.
And "not mind, not Buddha, not things" are the same.
So "what is, what is not mind?"
"Bring forth not mind and show it to me."
"Which buddha is this?"
"This is not buddha."
That's how we know he's buddha because he's not buddha.

So in Master Hongzu's manual of silent illumination, which was translated by Teigen Dan Leighton into "cultivating the empty field," he says, "An ancient said that not mind embodies and fulfills the way of not mind.
Embodying and fulfilling the way of not mind, finally you can rest.
Proceeding you are able to guide the assembly with thoughts clear, sitting silently, wander into the centre of the circle of wonder."
An ancient said that not mind embodies and fulfills the way of not mind.
Embodying and fulfilling the way of not mind, finally you can rest.
Proceeding you are able to guide the assembly with thoughts clear, sitting silently, wander into the centre of the circle of wonder.
So I could say the same about "not Buddha and not things."
"Not buddha embodies and fulfills the way of not buddha.
Embodying and fulfilling the way of not things, finally you can rest."
So it's not just a negation of mind, Buddha and things, it's actually practicing "not mind, not Buddha, not things."
Getting very close to mind, Buddha and things, and to "not mind, not Buddha, not things."
To embody and fulfill these ways.
And Mumun's verse on this koan kind of underlines that.
It says, "Talking too much spoils your virtue.
So I'm already in trouble.
Silence is truly unequaled.
Let the mountains become the sea, I'll give you no comment."
And of course, his "no comment" is a comment.
So I think that's probably a good place to end.
I've already talked too much and given up on my virtue.
"Talking too much spoils your virtue, silence is truly unequaled.
Let the mountains become the sea, I'll give you no comment."
Thank you very much.
Every being and place with the Tendam.
